reason: VY Canis Majoris features over 15 well-corroborated, dramatic facts across seven distinct sources detailing its colossal scale and violent eruptions.
story: In 1801, French astronomer Jérôme Lalande recorded a faint 7th-magnitude star in the constellation Canis Major: VY Canis Majoris. Located nearly 3,900 light-years from Earth, this extreme red hypergiant is one of the largest stars known in the Milky Way. With a radius estimated at 1,420 times that of the Sun, light takes six hours to travel around its equator, compared to just 14.5 seconds for our Sun. If placed at the center of our solar system, its surface would extend far beyond the orbit of Jupiter. VY Canis Majoris sheds mass at one of the highest rates known, throwing out giant knots and arcs of gas and dust during massive surface outbursts. Astronomer Roberta Humphreys described its violent eruptions as 'Betelgeuse on steroids.' These ejections block its light, causing deep dimming episodes lasting years. Nearing the end of its life, this hypergiant may explode as a supernova or collapse directly into a black hole.
angle: Light takes 14.5 seconds to circle our Sun, but would take six full hours to circle VY Canis Majoris—a hypergiant so vast it would swallow the orbit of Jupiter.

claims.claim: VY Canis Majoris is an extreme red hypergiant star located in the constellation Canis Major.
The star is located approximately 3,700 to 3,900 light-years away from Earth.
French astronomer Jérôme Lalande recorded the first known observation of VY Canis Majoris in 1801.
Interferometric observations estimate the radius of VY Canis Majoris to be about 1,420 times that of the Sun.
If placed at the center of the Solar System, VY Canis Majoris would extend beyond the orbit of Jupiter.
An object traveling at the speed of light would take 6 hours to circle VY Canis Majoris, compared to 14.5 seconds for the Sun.
VY Canis Majoris is between 178,000 and 300,000 times more luminous than the Sun.
The star has an estimated current mass of approximately 17 times that of the Sun.
VY Canis Majoris has an estimated surface temperature of about 3,490 Kelvin (around 5,820 degrees Fahrenheit).
19th-century observers mistook bright knots in the surrounding nebula for discrete companion stars.
VY Canis Majoris loses mass at one of the highest rates known for any star.
Massive ejections of gas and dust from surface activity create knots and arcs that temporarily obscure the star, causing years-long dimming episodes.
Astrophysicist Roberta Humphreys described VY Canis Majoris as behaving like 'Betelgeuse on steroids'.
Molecules such as water (H2O) and carbon monoxide (CO) have been detected in the cloud surrounding the star.
VY Canis Majoris is expected to end its life by exploding as a supernova or collapsing directly into a black hole.

disputed: Whether VY Canis Majoris reaches out to Saturn's orbit: earlier general statements suggest it extends toward Saturn (S2, S5), but precise modern radius measurements (1,420 solar radii) place its surface beyond Jupiter but short of Saturn (S1, S6, S7). Attribute modern size strictly as extending past Jupiter's orbit.

Historical size estimates: older calculations estimated sizes exceeding 2,800 to 3,000 solar radii, whereas modern interferometry refined the radius to ~1,420 solar radii (S1, S4, S6, S7). Frame modern 1,420 R☉ as the accepted measured size.

Initial mass: evolutionary models estimate initial mass between 25-32 solar masses (S1, S6, S7), while other sources state 35-40 solar masses (S2, S5, S6). Present as roughly 25 to 40 solar masses at birth.
